items.title: A 99% accurate medical test for a rare disease usually gives a false positive
items.claim: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate (1% false positive rate, 1% false negative rate). The disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have the disease? Roughly 1%, not 99%.

options.text: Base rate matters. Out of 10,000 random people: ~1 truly has the disease (and tests positive); ~100 don't have it but test positive anyway (1% of 9999). Total positives ~101, true positives 1. So P(disease given positive) ≈ 1/101 ≈ 1%
False positives are impossible for accurate tests

items.reveal:
Bayes's theorem: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) / P(positive).

P(positive | disease) = 0.99 (test sensitivity).
P(disease) = 0.0001 (base rate — the prevalence).
P(positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) + P(positive | no disease) * P(no disease) = 0.99 * 0.0001 + 0.01 * 0.9999 ≈ 0.0001 + 0.01 = 0.0101.
P(disease | positive) = 0.99 * 0.0001 / 0.0101 ≈ 0.0098 = 0.98%.

The 'accuracy' of the test is misleading when the disease is rare. The vast majority of positives are FALSE positives, drawn from the much larger pool of healthy people.

Key insight: rare conditions produce rare true positives. Even excellent tests produce overwhelming numbers of false positives in screening contexts.

Real-world implications:
- Mass screening for rare cancers, HIV, etc., requires careful interpretation of positives.
- Drug tests at low real-prevalence give many false accusations.
- Airport security: very low base rate of terrorists; almost all positives are false alarms.
- Mammograms in the 40-49 age group: famous case of low base rate leading to controversy over screening recommendations.

Professionals routinely misinterpret. Gigerenzer's studies show many doctors get this wrong on similar problems. Communicating in 'natural frequencies' (1 in 10,000) rather than probabilities (0.0001) helps people reason correctly.
items.why: Test accuracy seems to translate directly to confidence in results. Bayes's theorem forces a different interpretation: when the condition is rare, even sensitive tests produce mostly false positives. Whole branches of medicine and public policy depend on getting this right.

items.title: Bayesians and frequentists disagree about what probability even MEANS
items.claim: A frequentist says P(rain tomorrow) is undefined — tomorrow happens once. A Bayesian says P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 because that's their degree of belief. Two schools, two interpretations, often the same answers in practice.

options.text: Frequentist probability is long-run frequency of repeatable events; Bayesian probability is degree of belief / credibility. The Bayesian framework can attach probabilities to one-off events (tomorrow's weather, an election outcome) that frequentists consider non-probabilistic

items.reveal:
FREQUENTIST view: probability is the long-run frequency of an event in repeated trials. P(heads) = 1/2 means: in many flips, the proportion of heads approaches 1/2.
For one-off events ('rain tomorrow', 'this defendant is guilty', 'the next president will be X'), probability is undefined.

BAYESIAN view: probability is degree of belief. P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 means a rational degree of certainty. You can attach probabilities to anything you can think about — including one-off events.

Practical differences:
- Bayesians use prior distributions to incorporate background knowledge. Frequentists generally don't.
- Bayesians update priors with data via Bayes's theorem. Frequentists test null hypotheses (often binary accept/reject decisions).
- Frequentists ask: 'How likely is this data under H_0?' (the p-value).
- Bayesians ask: 'Given this data, what's the probability that H_0 is true?'

Most practitioners now use both depending on the problem. Frequentist tools dominate clinical trials, particle physics 'discovery thresholds' (sigma counts). Bayesian methods dominate machine learning, weather forecasting, medical diagnosis, search engines.

Historical context: frequentists dominated the 20th century. Bayesian methods were marginal until computational power (MCMC) made them practical in the 1990s. Since then, Bayesian methods have flourished.

The 'Bayesian vs frequentist' war was largely about philosophical foundations. In practice, most working statisticians now use whichever approach fits the problem best.

Edge cases: low-data or one-off events strongly favour Bayesian thinking. Repeatable experiments with lots of data give similar answers either way.
items.why: Two centuries of debate about what probability means produced two distinct philosophies, both useful for different problems. Anyone using statistics professionally needs to understand which framework they're working in.

items.title: Just 23 people give a 50/50 chance of a shared birthday
items.claim: How many people do you need in a room for it to be more likely than not that two share a birthday? Most people guess 100 or 180. The answer is 23.
items.prompt: Why is the threshold so low?

options.text: With 23 people there are 23 choose 2 = 253 possible pairs, each with about a 1/365 chance of matching; the question is not 'matches me' but 'any match anywhere', which has many more chances
Coincidences happen because of cosmic alignment

items.reveal:
The probability that NO two people in a group of n share a birthday is (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)...((365-n+1)/365).

For n = 23, this product equals about 0.493. Probability of AT LEAST ONE match equals 1 - 0.493 = 0.507. Just over 50 percent.
For n = 41, probability of a match is about 90 percent.
For n = 70, about 99.9 percent.

Intuition fails because we ask 'does someone share MY birthday?' — that requires n ≈ 253 for 50 percent. The real question allows ANY pair to match, and the number of pairs grows as n choose 2 ≈ n squared / 2.

This 'birthday attack' is important in cryptography: collision resistance of a hash function with N possible outputs only protects against attackers who try fewer than about square root of N inputs. A 128-bit hash gives only 64-bit collision security.
items.why: Counting pairs is qualitatively different from counting people. Pair counts grow quadratically, so coincidences are far more likely than a head-count suggests.
